input.description: Rebuild simplify with new convex_intersect sub-timers

content.text:
Clean build. Here's the new instrumented hierarchy under `intersect`:

```
├─ intersect                          …
│   ├─ copy_verts                     …   (Polygon → vector<Point> conversion in the wrapper)
│   └─ convex_intersect               …   (O'Rourke's main routine)
│       ├─ main_loop_body             …   (per-iteration: branching, advance, output appends)
│       ├─ sgn_tests                  …   (per-iteration: 2× area_sign, 1× area_sign_vec, 1× seg_seg_int)
│       ├─ post_hull                  …   (final CGAL::convex_hull_2 on `out`)
│       ├─ setup                      …   (signed-area winding fix + leftmost search, paid once)
│       └─ containment                …   (point_in_convex_poly on the no-crossing closure path)
```

What I'd expect the hot path to look like, and what each phase tells you:

| Phase | Per-call cost model | What's actually in it |
|---|---|---|
| `sgn_tests` | O(1) per loop iteration, 4 exact predicates | `area_sign_vec(A, B)` + 2× `area_sign` (triangle orient) + `seg_seg_int` (which itself calls `CGAL::intersection` on two `Kernel::Segment_2`s, plus 2 `squared_distance` for the `v`/`1` disambiguation, and `parallel_int` on the collinear path with up to 6 `between` checks each = up to 12 orientation calls). |
| `main_loop_body` | O(1) per iteration, plus one `out.push_back` per `1`/`v` | Branching on `code/cross/aHB/bHA`, `dot_sign` on `e`-overlap, `advance`, `in_out`, occasional `out.push_back`. |
| `copy_verts` | O(|P| + |Q|) | The two `vertices_begin/vertices_end` loops in the `intersect` wrapper. |
| `setup` | O(|P| + |Q|) but paid once per call | `signed_area` (O(|P|) and O(|Q|) of `Kernel::FT` multiplies — these are *exact* FT multiplies, so they can be a hidden cost) + `leftmost_index` (O(|P|) and O(|Q|) of `compare_y`/`compare_x`). |
| `post_hull` | O(k log k) | `CGAL::convex_hull_2` on the `out` points. Usually small k. |
| `containment` | O(|Q|) or O(|P|) | Only paid on the "boundaries don't cross" path; per-iteration cost is one full point-in-polygon scan. |

Optimization targets, in order of likely payoff:

1. **`setup` — `signed_area` uses `Kernel::FT`** (line 178: `s += (a.x() * b.x()...)`). With the `Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions_kernel`, the points are *stored* as doubles but the `*` is on `Kernel::FT`, which in this kernel is double — so this is fine. The `leftmost_index` is also `double` arithmetic. So setup is probably small, not a hotspot.

2. **`sgn_tests` — `seg_seg_int`** is the costliest of the four: it goes through `CGAL::intersection(Segment, Segment)`, which dispatches to a kernel-level segment intersection that internally computes ~3-4 predicates. Plus it does *additional* `squared_distance` checks to disambiguate `'1'` vs `'v'`, which is one exact-predicate `orientation` plus two `squared_distance`s. If we know the algorithm only uses `code == '1'` (proper crossing) and `code == 'v'` (endpoint touch) — and 'e' (overlap) is only relevant for the shared-edge early-out — we can rewrite `seg_seg_int` to avoid the variant-dispatch on `std::variant<Point, Segment>` and just do an O'Rourke-style `area_sign` of the two triangles plus a `between` check. That cuts out 2 `squared_distance`s and the variant discriminant per iteration.

3. **`main_loop_body`** — the `if (inflag == InFlag::Pin)` checks inside `advance` are dead-on-arrival reads of `inflag`; if your compiler doesn't hoist them, store the decision once. But really the only work is an `out.push_back` (when emitting) and the `% n` / `% m` advance — these are cheap.

4. **`copy_verts`** — easy win: a CGAL `Polygon` is already a sequence of points; you can construct the `std::vector<Point>` directly via `std::vector<Point>(subject.begin(), subject.end())` once the Polygon type is known to be `CGAL::Polygon_2<K, std::vector<Point>>` (it is). That removes 2 explicit loops and lets the compiler use memcpy/memmove for the underlying storage. Same for `clip`.

5. **`containment`** — only fires when `inflag == Unknown && first_point`, which is the "no crossings, possibly contained" path. Not called in the hot path, only in the closure. Unlikely to matter.

6. **`post_hull`** — `convex_hull_2` on a small `out` is O(k log k), k small. Unlikely to matter.

Most likely the dominant sub-timer will be `sgn_tests`; if so, the targeted rewrite of `seg_seg_int` (drop the variant, just do `orientation` + `between`) is the first thing to try. If it turns out to be `copy_verts`, the range-ctor swap is a one-liner. Run the benchmark and we'll see which it is.

void    ConvexIntersect( tPolygoni P, tPolygoni Q, int n, int m )

      SubVec( P[a], P[a1], A );
      SubVec( Q[b], Q[b1], B );

      aHB   = AreaSign( Q[b1], Q[b], P[a] );

      printf("%%cross=%d, aHB=%d, bHA=%d\n", cross, aHB, bHA );

      /* If A & B intersect, update inflag. */

      printf("%%SegSegInt: code = %c\n", code );

         printf("%%InOut sets inflag=%d\n", inflag);
      }

      /*-----Advance rules-----*/

      /* Special case: A & B overlap and oppositely oriented. */
      if ( ( code == 'e' ) && (Dot( A, B ) < 0) )
            PrintSharedSeg( p, q ), exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);

      /* Special case: A & B parallel and separated. */
      if ( (cross == 0) && ( aHB < 0) && ( bHA < 0 ) )

            else
               a = Advance( a, &aa, n, inflag == Pin, P[a] );
         }

      /* Generic cases. */
      else if ( cross >= 0 ) {
         if ( bHA > 0)
            a = Advance( a, &aa, n, inflag == Pin, P[a] );
         else
            b = Advance( b, &ba, m, inflag == Qin, Q[b] );

      else /* if ( cross < 0 ) */{

            b = Advance( b, &ba, m, inflag == Qin, Q[b] );
         else
            a = Advance( a, &aa, n, inflag == Pin, P[a] );
      }
      printf("%%After advances:a=%d, b=%d; aa=%d, ba=%d; inflag=%d\n", a, b, aa, ba, inflag);

   /* Quit when both adv. indices have cycled, or one has cycled twice. */
   } while ( ((aa < n) || (ba < m)) && (aa < 2*n) && (ba < 2*m) );

   if ( !FirstPoint ) /* If at least one point output, close up. */
            printf("%8.2lf %8.2lf lineto\n", p0[X], p0[Y] );

{

    if      ( area2 >  0.5 ) return  1;

/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
SegSegInt: Finds the point of intersection p between two closed
segments ab and cd.  Returns p and a char with the following meaning:
   'e': The segments collinearly overlap, sharing a point.
   'v': An endpoint (vertex) of one segment is on the other segment,
        but 'e' doesn't hold.
   '1': The segments intersect properly (i.e., they share a point and
        neither 'v' nor 'e' holds).
   '0': The segments do not intersect (i.e., they share no points).
Note that two collinear segments that share just one point, an endpoint
of each, returns 'e' rather than 'v' as one might expect.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
char	SegSegInt( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c, tPointi d, tPointd p, tPointd q )
{
   double  s, t;       /* The two parameters of the parametric eqns. */
   double num, denom;  /* Numerator and denoninator of equations. */
   char code = '?';    /* Return char characterizing intersection. */

   /*printf("%%SegSegInt: a,b,c,d: (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d)\n",
	a[X],a[Y], b[X],b[Y], c[X],c[Y], d[X],d[Y]);*/

   denom = a[X] * (double)( d[Y] - c[Y] ) +
           b[X] * (double)( c[Y] - d[Y] ) +
           d[X] * (double)( b[Y] - a[Y] ) +
           c[X] * (double)( a[Y] - b[Y] );

   /* If denom is zero, then segments are parallel: handle separately. */
   if (denom == 0.0)
      return  ParallelInt(a, b, c, d, p, q);

   num =    a[X] * (double)( d[Y] - c[Y] ) +
            c[X] * (double)( a[Y] - d[Y] ) +
            d[X] * (double)( c[Y] - a[Y] );
   if ( (num == 0.0) || (num == denom) ) code = 'v';
   s = num / denom;
   /*printf("num=%lf, denom=%lf, s=%lf\n", num, denom, s);*/

   num = -( a[X] * (double)( c[Y] - b[Y] ) +
            b[X] * (double)( a[Y] - c[Y] ) +
            c[X] * (double)( b[Y] - a[Y] ) );
   if ( (num == 0.0) || (num == denom) ) code = 'v';
   t = num / denom;
   /*printf("num=%lf, denom=%lf, t=%lf\n", num, denom, t);*/

   if      ( (0.0 < s) && (s < 1.0) &&
             (0.0 < t) && (t < 1.0) )
     code = '1';
   else if ( (0.0 > s) || (s > 1.0) ||
             (0.0 > t) || (t > 1.0) )
     code = '0';

   p[X] = a[X] + s * ( b[X] - a[X] );
   p[Y] = a[Y] + s * ( b[Y] - a[Y] );

   return code;
}
char   ParallelInt( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c, tPointi d, tPointd p, tPointd q )
{
/*   
   printf("ParallelInt: a,b,c,d: (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d)\n",
	a[X],a[Y], b[X],b[Y], c[X],c[Y], d[X],d[Y]);
*/

   if ( !Collinear( a, b, c) )
      return '0';

   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( a, b, d ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, c );
      Assigndi( q, d );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( c, d, a ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, a );
      Assigndi( q, b );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, c );
      Assigndi( q, b );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( c, d, a ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, c );
      Assigndi( q, a );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( a, b, d ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, d );
      Assigndi( q, b );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( a, b, d ) && Between( c, d, a ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, d );
      Assigndi( q, a );
      return 'e';
   }
   return '0';
}

bool    Between( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c )
{

   if ( a[X] != b[X] )

## O'Rourke fixed

The bug was that the previous O'Rourke was missing the **disjoint check** (cross == 0 && aHB < 0 && bHA < 0) and had a buggy "convex hull post-process" that was clipping out valid intersection vertices. The state machine was also exiting early (via `break`) on shared edges, then doing extra work that was sometimes wrong.

**What I changed** in `convex_intersect`:
1. Removed the `convex_hull_2` post-process (it was under-approximating when the O'Rourke output had a non-trivial shape)
2. Added the **disjoint check** (parallel + separated) — returns `{}` early
3. Replaced the `break` for shared edges with an immediate return of the shared-edge segment
4. The `inflag == Unknown && first_point` containment check is now done via `first_point` alone (no need to check inflag)
5. The shared-edge case no longer needs the `shared_edge` flag

**Verification:**
- `id=1`: 1028 points, Frechet 300.007, **MD5 matches `simplify.orourke.bak.txt` byte-for-byte**
- `id=10`: 484 points, Frechet 300.005

**Trade-off:**
- Time: 32s for id=1 (was 90s with the buggy O'Rourke, 3s with boost, 35s with HEAD's `long double` algorithm)
- Correctness: matches the .bak exactly
- The O'Rourke is still slower than boost because each call costs ~0.2ms in Epeck orientation tests; the boost version uses doubles and is ~10x faster

If you want it faster, the cleanest option is to use `boost::geometry::intersection` (3s) — I can do that as a follow-up. But for now the O'Rourke state machine is working and producing the correct output.

## Summary

**Root cause of the inflation bug:** In `simplify.cpp`, the `intersect()` wrapper (around line 386) checks `if (!inter_poly.is_simple()) return;` and silently drops the intersection if the polygon isn't simple. But O'Rourke's `convex_intersect` can output chains with **collinear or duplicate vertices** that fail CGAL's `is_simple_2` check (e.g., the first three vertices of an O'Rourke output are often collinear, which is fine geometrically but the CGAL `Polygon` constructor asserts `is_simple`). When the wrapper drops the intersection, `new_S[i]` stays empty, the cell gets marked dead, and the segment terminates.

With (delta=120.5, epsilon=0.8), this happened for every grid point after the first input point, so the algorithm was processing 1 input point per segment, doubling the output.

**Fix:** Added a collinear-vertex cleanup pass in `intersect()` that drops any vertex that coincides with or is collinear with its predecessor, looping until no change. For a convex polygon this strictly tightens the chain without changing the underlying region.

**Results** (for id=4, e=0.8):

| delta | before | after | Fréchet before | Fréchet after |
|------:|-------:|------:|---------------:|--------------:|
| 120.5 | 1068 pts | 82 pts | 183.64 | 183.64 |
| 10000 | 1344 pts | 2 pts | 15231.5 | 14142.1 |

For d=10000 the algorithm now correctly produces just 2 points (the whole trajectory fits in one segment), and the Fréchet bound (1.4 * delta) is respected.

**Why I didn't apply the other two "fixes":** I tried them but they all broke the Fréchet. The original `buffer[0] = P[i]` + `buffer[1] = first vertex of new_S` keeps both output points on the grid, within GRID distance of the input, so the polyline is dense and the Fréchet is preserved. Using `p0` or `last_pi` directly made the polyline have long segments with gaps, blowing the Fréchet to 200-14000. So the minimum-viable fix is just the collinear cleanup.
